name: Seed cycling

lead: Seed cycling is a food-based routine in which people eat flax and pumpkin seeds in the first half of the cycle and sesame and sunflower seeds in the second half. Followers say it supports hormonal balance, and through that, clearer skin and steadier cycles.

It has spread through wellness media. A 2025 systematic review of ten small studies reported possible benefits for menstrual symptoms and hormone markers, and its authors called for larger randomized trials.

paras: Practitioners describe about one to two tablespoons of ground seeds a day, switching seeds at mid-cycle, with some following the moon for irregular cycles. Seeds are added to smoothies or yogurt; capsules also exist. Followers usually continue for several months.

Seeds are ordinary foods, so risks are mainly allergies and digestive upset. Researchers note that evidence is limited, and clinicians stress that persistent cycle problems or PCOS warrant medical evaluation.

angle.text: People follow it hoping that steadier hormones will reduce hormonal acne and cycle-linked skin changes. The skin link is mostly claimed by advocates; research has focused on PMS and PCOS.

lead: Seed cycling is a wellness practice that rotates seeds across the menstrual cycle: flax and pumpkin seeds in the follicular phase, sesame and sunflower seeds in the luteal phase. Followers hope it will regulate cycles and ease PMS, and some also link it to acne and skin clarity.[1]

The idea rests on the lignans in flax, which have phytoestrogenic properties, and on seed nutrients that advocates say gently influence hormone production.[1] Wikipedia does not date its origin; media coverage has ranged from sceptical to enthusiastic.[1]
Published research includes a 2025 systematic review of ten studies (635 participants) and small trials in PCOS.[2][3]

paras: Proponents divide the cycle into a follicular phase (about days 1 to 14) and luteal phase (about days 15 to 28), assigning flax and pumpkin to the first and sesame and sunflower to the second, in roughly one to two tablespoons of ground seed daily. For irregular cycles, some follow the lunar calendar.[1]
Advocates say flax lignans and seed minerals support estrogen and progesterone balance, with benefits for PMS, cycle regularity, acne and mood.[1]

A 2025 systematic review in Cureus covered ten studies (635 participants) of seed cycling or its component seeds in PMS and PCOS, and reported associations with improved hormone and symptom measures, particularly for flax and sesame, while calling for larger randomized trials.[2][1]

A 2023 study in 90 women with PCOS compared control, diet plus metformin, and diet plus seed cycling groups over 12 weeks and reported hormone changes in the seed group.[4] A 2024 open-label study of 32 women with PCOS and a single-arm trial of seed cycling capsules with chasteberry over two cycles have also been reported, along with a case report on PCOS and infertility.[5][6][7] An animal study in healthy rats examined seed mixtures across the estrous cycle.[8]
Outlets such as The Telegraph, The Cut and Good Housekeeping have been sceptical, while WWD, Harper's Bazaar and Vogue Arabia covered it as a wellness trend.[1]

lore.intro: Seed cycling is discussed on wellness and women's health media as a gentle, food-based way to support hormones and skin.[1]

claims.claim: Flax and pumpkin early, sesame and sunflower late, balances estrogen and progesterone
